note.text:
To solve a cubic equation f(x) = 0:
1. Make one side 0.
2. Factorise f(x) completely (Lesson 14).
3. Set each factor equal to 0.
A cubic equation has at most three real roots.
Example: x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = 0 → (x − 1)(x − 3)(x + 2) = 0 → x = 1, 3 or −2.
If x is a common factor, take it out; never divide by x: x³ = 4x → x(x − 2)(x + 2) = 0 → x = 0, 2 or −2.
If the quadratic factor has a negative discriminant, it gives no real roots, and the cubic has only one.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to solve a cubic equation by factorising, find all its real roots, and say when there is only one.
Builds on: Lesson {14} (factorising cubics) and Lesson {7} (solving by factorisation).
Leads to: drawing cubic graphs, where the roots are the points on the x-axis.

sections.heading: Three factors, three roots
sections.text:
Once a cubic equation is factorised, the rule from Lesson {7} still works: if a product is {0}, a factor is {0}.
Solve {cubic(1, -2, -5, 6)} = {0}.
• f({1}) = {0}, so (x − {1}) is a factor; dividing gives {quad(1, -1, -6)} = (x − {3})(x + {2}).
• (x − {1})(x − {3})(x + {2}) = {0}, so x = {1}, x = {3} or x = {-2}.
Take x out first if every term has an x: x³ − {mono(9, 'x')} = x(x − {3})(x + {3}) = {0} gives x = {0}, {3}, {-3}.

sections.heading: Fewer than three roots
sections.text:
Sometimes the quadratic factor does not factorise. Check its discriminant.
• (x − {2})({quad(1, 1, 3)}) = {0}: for the quadratic, b² − {4}ac = {1} − {12} = {-11}, negative.
• So it has no real roots, and the only solution is x = {2}.
If the discriminant is positive but not a square number, use the formula (Lesson {10}) for the last two roots.

worked_example.problem: Solve {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)} = {0}.
steps: Each factor can be {0}: x − {p} = {0}, x − {q} = {0} or x + {-r} = {0}.

cards.idea: When a cubic is written as three factors equal to {0}, each factor gives a root.
Take out x as a common factor instead of dividing by x.
If the quadratic factor has b² − {4}ac < {0}, it has no real roots.

distractors.text: x = {p}, and two more roots from the quadratic

misconceptions.explain: Check the quadratic: b² − {4}ac = {b * b - 4 * c} is negative, so it has no real roots.
The bracket x − {br(p)} still gives the root x = {p}.

solution: For {quad(1, b, c)}: b² − {4}ac = {b * b} − {4 * c} = {b * b - 4 * c} < {0}, so it has no real roots.

questions.prompt: Solve {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)} = {0}. Give the largest root.

misconceptions.explain: The roots have the opposite signs to the numbers in the brackets.

solution: Try factors of {-p * q * r} to find one root, divide, and factorise the quadratic.
The roots are {p}, {q}, {r}; the largest is {answer}.

questions.prompt: x = {p} is a root of {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)} = {0}. Find the other two roots and give the smaller one.

misconceptions.explain: The roots are opposite in sign to the numbers in the brackets.
x = {p} is the root you were given. The question asks for one of the other two.

solution: ({poly([1, 'x'], [-p, ''])}) is a factor. Dividing gives {quad(1, -(q + r), q * r)}.
The other roots are {q} and {r}; the smaller is {answer}.
where: p < min(q, r) || p > min(q, r)
